system.name: MSP430FR
system.one_liner: a commercial energy-harvesting microcontroller platform combining volatile and non-volatile memory for intermittent computing

components.name: Harvester

components.name: Capacitor
components.role: stores harvested energy, typically a few to several hundred microfarads

content.key_idea: An energy-harvesting platform gathers ambient energy into a capacitor to power an ultra-low-power MCU, which has both volatile memory (lost on power failure) and non-volatile memory (persists across power cycles).
content.reading_order: Left to right: a harvester charges a capacitor that powers the MCU, which connects to volatile memory (blue, at risk) and non-volatile memory (green, persistent).

summary: This figure is background context (not the paper's own INTOS system, shown separately in Figure 2) illustrating the generic hardware architecture of an energy-harvesting platform such as the TI MSP430FR. A harvester gathers ambient energy such as solar or RF and stores it in a capacitor, typically sized from a few to several hundred microfarads. The capacitor powers an ultra-low-power MCU, which the caption notes is often built with a 16 MHz core, 8KB SRAM, and 256KB FRAM in the concrete MSP430FR5994 example. The MCU connects to Volatile Memory (e.g. SRAM, shown in blue) and Non-Volatile Memory (e.g. FRAM/MRAM, shown in green); registers and SRAM are highlighted in blue specifically because they are lost whenever the capacitor's charge is depleted and power is interrupted, motivating the paper's discussion of crash-consistency techniques.
summary_zh: 该图为背景图，展示能量采集平台（如 MSP430FR）架构：采集器收集环境能量存入电容为 MCU 供电，MCU 连接易失性内存（蓝，断电丢失）与非易失性内存（绿，断电保留）。
notes: layout-proposal: linear hardware block diagram — a simple left-to-right energy/data flow (harvester to capacitor to MCU to memories) with no processing stages; pipeline is kept as the closest named template though the fit is loose. This is generic background on energy-harvesting hardware, not INTOS itself (INTOS is shown in Fig. 2).
